title: A contract test that catches Square extends Rectangle

blocks.text: LSP says an object of a subtype must be usable wherever its base type is, without breaking the program. The page's classic violation is `Square extends Rectangle`:
`Rectangle`'s contract is that `setWidth(w)` changes only the width and `setHeight(h)` only the height. `Contracts` already holds `Rectangle` and the page's `Square`.

Write `honoursRectangleContract(Rectangle r)`, a **contract test**: it runs the page's client code on `r`, in the page's order (`setWidth(5)`, then `setHeight(3)`), and returns `true` only when, after that, `getWidth()` is `5`, `getHeight()` is `3` and `area()` is `15`. It reads the object only through those public methods, as any client would: a subclass may keep its sides somewhere else.

items: `new Rectangle(1, 1)` honours it, and `new Square(4)` does not.

It judges **behaviour, not type**: a subclass written later that breaks the contract is caught, and one that keeps it is accepted. Checking `instanceof Square`, or the exact class, is the smell the page warns about, not a test.
A subtype can get any one of the three answers wrong while the other two look right, so all three are checked.

cases.says: Rectangles honour the contract and Square(4) does not.
A subclass that ignores setHeight is caught, although it is not a Square.
A subclass whose setHeight swaps the sides has area 15 and still fails the contract.
A subclass that counts its resizes and keeps the contract is accepted.
A subclass whose setHeight quietly changes the width to 4 (with area still 15) breaks the contract: the width is read after both calls.

concepts: Square extends Rectangle breaks Rectangle's contract, because setting the width also changes the height, so code written for a Rectangle gets the wrong area.
LSP is checked by running code written against the base type's behaviour on any subtype; special-casing a subtype with instanceof is the smell, not the test.
